here are some excessive notes. can you help me decide what sliders to add for getting the best possible VMT denominators?

---

Goal: bound ADS-engaged vehicle miles traveled (VMT) in the US, 2025-06-15 thru 2025-12-15, for a given operator, matching NHTSA SGO ADS incidents filtered to Driver/Operator Type = None.

Define:

* D = denominator miles you want = total US public-road miles with ADS engaged, in-scope, during the window.

Global/common parameters (apply to all operators)

* Geographic scope fraction:

   * f_US = fraction of the operator’s reported ADS miles that occurred in the US (if the reported metric is global).

* Road-scope fraction:

   * f_public = fraction of those US miles that occurred on “publicly accessible roads” (exclude closed-course, private lots, depots).

* ADS-engaged fraction:

   * f_ADS = fraction of the operator’s reported miles that are truly “ADS engaged” as defined by SGO (as opposed to manual driving, remote-only maneuvering, etc.), if the reported metric mixes modes.

* Operator=none mapping (only if your mileage source mixes operator types):

   * f_none = fraction of ADS-engaged miles where Driver/Operator Type would be “None” (no driver responsible) as opposed to in-vehicle safety driver / remote operator / test driver.
   * If you already have a mileage metric that is explicitly “driverless / rider-only / no driver,” set f_none = 1.

Service vs non-service decomposition parameters

* Deadhead/empty-mile share:

* d = non-service share of ADS-engaged VMT (0..1), where:

  * VMT_total = VMT_service + VMT_nonservice
  * d = VMT_nonservice / VMT_total
* Equivalently, multiplier from service miles to total VMT:

  * m_deadhead = 1 / (1 - d)
  * VMT_total = VMT_service * m_deadhead
* If you have total VMT directly, you don’t need d.

* If you only have passenger-miles (or “rider-only miles”) instead of vehicle-miles:

   * o = average vehicle occupancy during service (passenger count per vehicle-mile while in service), to convert:

     * passenger_miles = VMT_service * o
     * VMT_service = passenger_miles / o
   * If your service-mile metric is already vehicle-miles (not passenger-miles), set o = 1 and ignore.

Operator-specific “base-mile” parameter (choose one per operator)
8) Base mileage metric in-window before applying the fractions above (you need at least one of these):

* B_totalVMT: reported ADS vehicle-miles (service + non-service) in-window, OR
* B_serviceVMT: reported ADS vehicle-miles with customers (service miles) in-window, OR
* B_passengerMiles: reported passenger-miles in-window, OR
* B_cumulative(t): reported cumulative total at known dates t1 and t2 that bracket the window (so you can difference and/or interpolate).

Then compute bounds as:

* If B_totalVMT available:
  D = B_totalVMT * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none
* If only B_serviceVMT available:
  D = B_serviceVMT * m_deadhead * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none
* If only B_passengerMiles available:
  D = (B_passengerMiles / o) * m_deadhead * f_US * f_public * f_ADS * f_none

Minimum set needed to produce lower/upper bounds (typical)

* A base mileage metric B_* for the window (or bracketing cumulative values).
* d (deadhead share) unless B_totalVMT already includes non-service miles.
* f_none unless the base metric is explicitly driverless/no-driver.
* f_US if base metric isn’t US-only.
* f_public if base metric includes private/closed-course miles.
* f_ADS if base metric mixes ADS-engaged and non-ADS miles.
* o only if using passenger-miles instead of vehicle-miles.

don't change any code but to be apples-to-apples, should it be fine to just leave all the non-service-share sliders at 0% for each company?
02:45 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 20s

Yes, you can do that, with one caveat.

  • If you set all non-service share sliders to 0%, you’re comparing service/on-trip miles per incident consistently across companies.
  • That is apples-to-apples in that specific sense.

But:

  • Your numerator (NHTSA incidents) can include incidents during non-service miles too.
  • So 0% for all is not apples-to-apples for total ADS VMT; it will undercount denominators, and the bias is larger for companies with higher true deadhead.

So it’s fine if you interpret results as “per service mile.”
For “per total autonomous mile,” you should use nonzero deadhead assumptions.

does this model even make sense? can we rethink this from first principles?
03:15 Codex gpt-5.3-codex (xhigh) thought for 1m8s

Yes, we should rethink it from first principles.

  • Base model is coherent: if incidents are a Poisson process per mile, then with Jeffreys prior \(p(\lambda)\propto \lambda^{-1/2}\), posterior is \(\lambda \mid k,m \sim \text{Gamma}(k+0.5,\text{rate}=m)\).

This part in index.html:292–index.html:305 is conceptually fine, and the gammaquant numerics look accurate.

  • The phi part is the conceptual mismatch: index.html:294–index.html:295 scales both shape and rate by phi. That inflates variance, but because the UI uses 1 / median(lambda) as the point estimate (index.html:298, index.html:302), the center moves with phi.

So the current tooltip claim “higher values widen intervals” (index.html:408, etc.) is incomplete/wrong.

  • From first principles, overdispersion is not identifiable from one aggregate count per company. So the clean options are:
  1. Remove phi entirely (most principled with current data).
  2. Keep phi as a subjective “interval widen” control, but force center invariance (e.g., center at m/(k+0.5) and widen bounds around that center on log scale).

If you want, I can implement option 2 now and add a qual that fails if the point estimate changes when only phi changes.

  • Keep point estimate fixed (eg 1 / median(lambda)), independent of interval mass
  • Let slider control only interval tails: tail = (1 - mass)/2
  • Interval for miles/incident: [1/q_{1-tail}(lambda), 1/q_{tail}(lambda)]

Sanity check done against Kelsey Piper’s March 2026 article.

What matches vs doesn’t

| Metric | Kelsey framing | Crashla Waymo (Jun 15, 2025–Jan 15, 2026) | Crashla Waymo (Jun 15–Sep 30, 2025 only) | Verdict |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| “Any crash” | ~half human (inferred from Kusano/Scanlon: 2.1 vs 4.68 IPMM) | 4.77 IPMM (all incidents) | 5.51 IPMM (all incidents) | Discrepant if using all |
| Nonstationary crashes | (closest apples-to-apples to moving-crash framing) | 1.85 IPMM | 2.27 IPMM | Close to Kelsey’s “~half” framing |
| Injury | “~one-fifth as likely” | 0.524 IPMM | 0.641 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 13–19% depending benchmark) |
| Airbag deployment | “~one-fifth as likely” | 0.204 IPMM | 0.241 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 12–15%) |
| Serious injury (SSI+) | “~one-tenth as likely” | 0.029 IPMM | 0.027 IPMM | Broadly consistent (about 12%) |
| Fatal | Kelsey cites ~0.5 fatalities over 127M miles | 0.333 weighted fatalities over 103.1M effective miles = 0.00323 IPMM | 0.00891 IPMM | Same order, but method differs |

Why the discrepancies are real (not math bugs)

  1. Different window.

Kelsey’s Waymo figures are cumulative “through Sep 2025” (127M). Crashla is scoped to June 15, 2025 through January 15, 2026 and explicitly partial-month prorated. See [preprocess.py:172](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:172), [preprocess.py:498](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:498), [crashla.js:1265](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1265).

  1. Different numerator definition for “all”.

Crashla all uses all SGO incidents with operator None, including many stationary/0-mph events; Waymo has 301/492 at 0 mph in this window. Nonstationary is the closer analogue to Kelsey’s crash framing. See [crashla.js:1125](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1125).

  1. Different denominator definition.

Crashla uses modeled VMT (with coverage and incident-coverage adjustments), not Waymo’s published rider-only cumulative denominator.

  1. Fatality accounting is different by design.

Crashla uses per-vehicle fatality weighting (1 / vehiclesInvolved) and overrides the Sep 2025 Tempe fatality to 3 vehicles. See [preprocess.py:96](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/preprocess.py:96), [crashla.js:1236](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js:1236).

Net: the injury/airbag/serious-injury story is consistent with Kelsey’s order-of-magnitude claims. The apparent mismatch is mainly on all incidents, where Crashla’s all metric is broader and includes many stationary events; nonstationary aligns much better.

Sources:

  • https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/we-absolutely-do-know-that-waymos
  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12675
  • https://waymo.com/safety/impact/

Yes, that fatality mismatch is real, but it’s mostly an apples-to-oranges comparison, not a math bug.

Piper’s 3.2x comes from this setup:

  • Waymo: 127M miles / 0.5 fatalities ≈ 254M miles per fatality
  • Humans: ~80M miles per fatality
  • Multiplier: 254/80 ≈ 3.2x

Your Jun-Sep table used a different setup:

  • Denominator: 37.4M (only Jun 15–Sep 30 in this model, with June prorated)
  • Fatal numerator: 0.333 (per-vehicle weighting of the Sep fatal incident)
  • Plus Bayesian shrinkage for tiny k (posterior median), which pulls MPI down further

That’s why you see roughly 0.54x–0.94x in that specific table.

If you do Jun-Sep with Piper-style arithmetic (no prior, direct m/k), you get:

  • 37.4M / 0.333 ≈ 112M, so 112/80 ≈ 1.4x (not 0.94x)

And with the latest full window (Jun 15–Jan 15), Piper-style is even higher:

  • 103.1M / 0.333 ≈ 309M, so 309/80 ≈ 3.9x

So:

  1. Nonfatal metrics: no big contradiction; directionally consistent.
  2. Fatality: very sensitive to method/window; your displayed Jun-Sep number is not directly comparable to Piper’s 3.2x.

I initially categorized it as 0.0 fault because it sounded like an unpredictable/adversarial action by a pedestrian intentionally blocking the road.

However, after looking closer at the actual narrative logic, you make a great point:

"The Waymo AV was traveling northbound in the left lane on Main Street when it approached a wire apparently tied on one end to a utility pole and being held up by a pedestrian on the west sidewalk of Main Street, such that the wire was suspended low across all lanes... The Waymo proceeded straight, striking the suspended wire and then driving over it."

The wire was already stretched across all lanes when the AV approached it. This means the AV failed to detect a stationary physical obstacle in its path and drove straight into it (and over it). While the pedestrian created the hazard, fundamentally the AV's perception system failed a very basic driving task (don't drive into visible things obstructing the road). For contrast, Claude evaluated this as 50% fault, and Codex gave it 80% fault.

I've corrected this in to properly assign fault (1.0 AV fault for failing to detect the obstacle) and re-ran to regenerate the data file!

To answer your actual question about the biggest discrepancy between our app and Kelsey Piper's article:

Piper is evaluating Waymo's *all-time* safety record, whereas our app is strictly windowed to June 2025 – January 2026 (to ensure apples-to-apples baseline comparisons across the active window).

Because of this difference in time scope, the biggest discrepancies are:

  1. Fatalities: Piper notes Waymo has been present for *two* fatal incidents (a 3-car crash counting as 0.33 deaths, and a 7-car crash counting as 0.14 deaths, totaling 0.47). Because our dashboard only starts tracking from June 2025 forward, the 7-car crash isn't in our dataset. We only record the September 3-car motorcycle crash in Tempe, meaning our app assesses Waymo with 0.33 fatalities instead of 0.47.
  2. VMT Math: Piper notes that Waymo hit 127 million miles *all-time* as of September 2025. Because we only tally miles within the June–Jan window, our system uses an effective VMT of roughly ~106 million miles for Waymo's rates. (Coincidentally, our dataset projects Waymo's *in-window* cumulative mileage hitting ~127 million miles right at the end of January, but these represent two completely different mileages).

Otherwise, the rates and core arguments closely match. Our SGO dataset confirms Waymo has 1 serious injury per ~35 million miles (roughly the "one-tenth" of the human benchmark, as she cites) and 1 airbag deployment per ~5 million miles (far lower than the human rate, also matching her argument).

  • Total Miles Driven (VMT): The article estimates 800,000 total robotaxi miles for Tesla. Our cumulative metric (using Austin robotaxitracker data) projects a lower figure of 672,500 miles through the end of January 2026.
  • Crash Rate Implications: Because the article uses a higher mileage denominator (800,000 / 14), they get a collision rate of roughly 1 in every 57,000 miles. Our data points toward a slightly higher frequency of roughly 1 in every 48,035 miles (672,500 / 14).
  • The "First vs Last 7" Split: The author notes Tesla hit its first 7 collisions over about 250,000 miles and the next 7 over 550,000 miles. According to our timeline, Tesla crossed the 250k-mile threshold around the end of October 2025 (256,984 cumulative miles). By that point, our dataset already shows 8 collisions (3 in July, 4 in Sept, 1 in Oct) rather than 7.

18:33 Copilot Chat copilot/gemini-3.1-pro-preview thought for 1m3s

Here is a step-by-step breakdown of exactly what that command does:

  1. head -n 831 data/faultfrac-gemini.csv

This reads exactly the first 831 lines of the file and outputs them. (Anything from line 832 onward is ignored).

  1. > temp.csv

This redirects that output (the 831 lines) and saves it into a new temporary file named temp.csv.

  1. &&

This operator tells the terminal to only run the next part of the command *if* the first part succeeded without any errors.

  1. mv temp.csv data/faultfrac-gemini.csv

This moves (renames) temp.csv to overwrite .

The final result:
It permanently truncates so that it contains *only* its first 831 lines. Any data that existed on line 832 or below is completely deleted.

*(Note: In my previous cancelled command, I used head -n -20, where the minus sign means "keep everything *except* the last 20 lines". I was trying to surgically remove the last 20 corrupted lines I had accidentally appended, not keep only 20 lines! But using a text editor or being more careful is definitely safer.)*

One important nuance first: in our app the human “50% / 80% / 95%” fan is not three different intervals. For humans, all three bands are the same fixed lo..hi range in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L821). If you mean the All Locations row only, then the direct matches are basically inside:

  • Injury: Waymo human 3.90 IPMM = about 256k MPI, inside our 252k..524k band in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L255).
  • Airbag in any vehicle: 1.63 IPMM = about 613k MPI, inside our 500k..700k band in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L291).
  • Serious injury or worse: 0.22 IPMM = about 4.55M MPI, inside our 3.3M..6.7M band in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L308).

The one small exception is our hospitalization surrogate band in [crashla.js](/Users/dreeves/lab/crashla/crashla.js#L273): its upper end is 4.35M, but if you derive that upper endpoint from Waymo’s current all-location serious benchmark 0.22, you get about 4.55M, which is slightly outside.

If you include the per-city human benchmarks from Waymo, then several are outside our global bands:

  • San Francisco injury benchmark 7.47 IPMM = about 134k MPI, below our injury band.
  • Phoenix serious benchmark 0.10 IPMM = 10.0M MPI, above our serious band.
  • San Francisco serious benchmark 0.43 IPMM = about 2.33M MPI, below our serious band.
  • Airbag benchmarks are outside in multiple cities too:

Phoenix 1.35 -> 741k above,
Los Angeles 1.23 -> 813k above,
San Francisco 2.11 -> 474k below,
Austin 2.37 -> 422k below.

So the careful answer is:

  • All Locations only: almost no, except the hospitalization surrogate upper endpoint is a bit stale.
  • Anything on the Waymo page, including city rows: yes, definitely. Our human bands are too global to contain all of Waymo’s city-specific human benchmarks.

Source: Waymo Safety Impact.

Your nose is right that the two curves look discordant, but the cause isn't a bug — it's that VMT doesn't control the width at all. The width is set by the at-fault *count*, and Tesla and Zoox are nowhere near similar there.

The mechanism

The plotted curve is the inverse-Gamma density with shape α = k + 0.5 and rate β = VMT ([crashla.js:835-837](crashla.js#L835-L837)). On a log axis those two parameters do completely separate jobs:

  • β (VMT) sets horizontal position only. It's a pure scale factor — slide-left/slide-right. It never changes the curve's width. (Mathematically, the SD of log(rate) for a Gamma is sqrt(trigamma(α)), with no β in it.)
  • α = k + 0.5 (the at-fault count) sets the width. Fewer at-fault events → fatter curve.

So "Tesla and Zoox have similar cumulative VMT" predicts their curves sit at a *similar position if they had the same at-fault rate* — it says nothing about width.

The actual counts

| | at-fault mass k | α | VMT | log-axis width (geo SD) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla | 5.75 | 6.25 | ~2.4M | ×1.52 |
| Zoox | 0.5 | 1.0 | ~2.1M | ×3.61 |
| Waymo | 131 | 131.5 | ~172M | ×1.09 |

Tesla has ~11× more at-fault mass than Zoox (6 incidents judged near-fully-at-fault: [1,1,0.75,1,1,1], vs Zoox's lone [0.4, 0.1]). That's why Zoox's curve is 3.1× wider than Tesla's despite the near-identical mileage. Waymo's spike is narrow for the same reason in reverse — 131 at-fault events pin it down tightly. Do the thought experiment: hand Zoox Tesla's exact VMT and its curve doesn't narrow one bit — it just slides sideways.

The part actually worth chewing on

The counterintuitive kicker: Zoox has *more* total incidents than Tesla (35 vs 18), similar miles, and yet the *widest* at-fault curve of the three. More incidents don't narrow an at-fault estimate — only at-fault incidents do, and ~33 of Zoox's 35 were judged not-its-fault ([crashla.js:971](crashla.js#L971) sums faultfracs, not incidents). So the width is faithfully reporting "we have essentially two fault-bearing data points for Zoox." That's real, not smelly.

Where I'd still aim the suspicion (same as before): that width reflects *only* sampling noise on k. Zoox's VMT — the thing setting where the fat curve sits — is an explicit 0.5×–2× "rough est." placeholder, and the plotted curve ignores that band entirely (it uses vmtBest alone). So the curve is honestly wide about the at-fault rate and silently overconfident about the mileage. Both Tesla's narrowness and Zoox's width are computed correctly; the soft input is the denominator, not the shape.

Right — this is the design wart, and the code makes it explicit. At [crashla.js:835](crashla.js#L835) the density function is built from only two things:

const beta = metricVmtBest;                              // the POINT estimate
densityFn: x => invGammaLogDensity(x, alpha, beta),      // alpha = k + 0.5

The band-aware est (whose lo/hi come from vmtMin/vmtMax) is spread into the object too, but the curve only ever reads alpha and beta. So:

  • α = k + 0.5 (the at-fault count) sets the bell's width.
  • β = vmtBest (the point estimate) sets the bell's horizontal position — on a log axis it's a pure translation.
  • vmt_min/vmt_max (the band) feed nothing in the density. They go only into estimateMpiWindow's lo/hi, which is the *numeric CI on the card*, not the drawn curve.

So the bell is the posterior over true MPI conditional on VMT being exactly vmtBest. It conditions the VMT uncertainty away. That's why tightening the band moved the CI but not the curve.

Is that defensible? In effect yes, in principle no.

The variance of log(MPI) decomposes additively into an at-fault-count term and a VMT term:

(1) DRAWN bell 95% (at vmtBest):        569K – 83M
(2) PRINTED CI (VMT extremes):          398K – 108M
(3) PROPER marginal 95% (Monte Carlo):  521K – 80M

log-sd from k alone:    1.283   ← this is essentially the whole bell width
log-sd from VMT band:   0.179
log-sd if combined:     1.295   ← folding VMT in widens the bell ~1%

Two things fall out:

Folding VMT uncertainty into the bell would widen it ~1% now, ~5% even under the old 2× band. The bell is overwhelmingly an "α = half a data point" story; VMT is a rounding error on its *width* (it only really moves its *position*, via β — and that position is the well-anchored central estimate).
  1. The genuine inconsistency you smelled: there are *three* different "uncertainty" numbers for Zoox's at-fault MPI on screen, and they disagree. The drawn bell's own 95% (569K–83M), the printed CI (398K–108M), and the statistically-correct marginal (521K–80M) are all different. Faultfrac uncertainty model — the structure I think is right

Let me propose a decomposition, because it separates a parameter-free correctness fix from the genuinely hard part.

The faultfrac criterion is "P(an expert human would have avoided)" = P(the AV is at fault). So each incident is a *Bernoulli(p_i)*, and the true at-fault count is K = Σ Bernoulli(p_i) — a Poisson-binomial, not a known number. That gives two cleanly separated layers:

Layer 1 — aleatoric (parameter-free, and currently approximated wrong). Even if Claude's p_i are perfectly calibrated, K is random. The principled rate posterior is the *mixture*

posterior(λ) = Σ_K P(K | {p_i}) · Gamma(λ; K+0.5, VMT)

The code instead plugs E[K]=Σp_i into the shape: Gamma(Σp_i + 0.5, VMT). For Zoox that's Gamma(0.6), but the correct object is 0.9·Gamma(0.5) + 0.1·Gamma(1.5) — not the same distribution. This layer needs no free parameters, is exact given the p_i, and matters most exactly where data is thinnest. Let me show the gap:

The median/quantile numbers there are garbage — I left a lexicographic .sort() (string sort) in the MC, so only the P(safer) column is valid. Let me fix that and get correct quantiles before drawing any conclusion.

Fixed (numeric sort). Here's the corrected, valid comparison for Zoox at-fault:

| rate model | median | 95% CI | P(safer) |
|---|---|---|---|
| current Gamma(0.6) (Σp+0.5) | 6.82M | 735K – 1,241M | 100.0% |
| proper 0.9·Gamma(0.5) + 0.1·Gamma(1.5) | 7.73M | 691K – 3,590M | 99.9% |

So Layer 1 is real but modest: it shifts the median ~13% and roughly triples the upper-tail mass (the K=0 branch, 90% weight, is heavier-tailed than Gamma(0.6)), yet it doesn't budge the verdict — Zoox reads ~certainly-safer either way *at face value*. It's a parameter-free shape correction, principled, and it matters more where a verdict is close. Good to have, not where the action is.

Layer 2 is where "the principled thing" stops being knowable

The action — and the honesty — is in treating Claude's f_i as a noisy, possibly biased estimate of the true q_i, not as q_i itself:

q_i ~ Beta(κ·f_i, κ·(1−f_i)), then K = Σ Bernoulli(q_i), rate ~ Gamma(K+½, VMT)

Three knobs, in decreasing defensibility:

  • κ (trust in Claude's faultfrac): the master dial. κ→∞ = current behavior (Claude is exactly right). Smaller κ = more judgment uncertainty. *Nothing in our data pins κ.*
  • bias δ: is Claude systematically lenient or harsh toward AVs? A shift on every f_i. Also unpinnable without ground truth.
  • correlation ρ across incidents: if Claude errs the same way on similar narratives, errors don't average out. Moot for Zoox (1 in-window event), but decisive for Waymo (131) — correlated judgment error could move Waymo's aggregate at-fault count 10–30%, which is its whole comparison.

The whole pipeline then composes into one posterior: VMT prior (done, layer a) × Poisson-binomial K (layer 1) × judgment uncertainty (layer 2) × Gamma rate. (a) was the first brick; they share the same "build the posterior" machinery.

Good — looked at both. Here's what I found and think.

Q1: Are the faultfracs solid enough to treat as gospel?

Having read them: your instinct is right — they're solid. The distribution and the reasoning both hold up:

faultfrac     count
0             1333   (73%)  — AV stopped/legal, got hit; usually obvious
(0,0.2)        271          — "rear-ended while stopped", "minibike into lane, unavoidable"
[0.2,0.5)      133
[0.5,0.8)       39          — genuinely ambiguous ("struck cardboard debris, visibility ambiguous")
[0.8,1)         43
1               17   — clear AV fault ("clipped parked tow truck")

The 73% zeros are the easy, low-judgment-risk cases. The graded middle lands on genuinely ambiguous incidents where *any* rater would be uncertain — so a 0.5 is honestly capturing "could go either way," not arbitrariness. I don't see a lean in the samples.

But "treat as gospel, same as the hard NHTSA fields" needs one distinction. Injury/airbag/fatality are *reported facts* (structured, company-stated, NHTSA-coded). A faultfrac is an *interpretation of a free-text narrative the company wrote*. That's a softer epistemic category. The question is whether that softness actually matters, and the answer splits cleanly:

  • Random judgment noise → doesn't matter, treat as gospel. It averages out. Rough cut: ~500 nonzero faultfracs, per-incident judgment error maybe ±0.15 → aggregate error on the at-fault count ≈ √500 × 0.15 ≈ 2.5%. That's *third-order* next to the VMT band (±30%) and even the Poisson sampling (~9% for Waymo). So modeling per-incident judgment uncertainty — the elaborate Beta/κ model I sketched — is overkill. It would carefully propagate a uncertainty that's already in the noise.
  • Systematic lean → the one real "gospel risk", and it does *not* average out. If the criterion or Claude is consistently, say, 15% too lenient toward AVs, every at-fault count is 15% low and it flows straight into the conclusions. We can't detect this without ground truth.

The good news: you already have the right tool for the only risk that matters. faultFlipMultiplier asks exactly "how far off (multiplicatively) would the at-fault mass have to be to flip the verdict?" Per AGENTS.md it's ~3.75× for Waymo and ~6.31× for Tesla — i.e., the verdicts survive a *275–530% systematic lean*, which is wildly larger than any plausible bias. So the verdicts are robust to the gospel risk.

My recommendation: treat the faultfracs as gospel for the point estimate (they're solid, and their noise is dominated by uncertainties you already carry), and lean on the flip-multiplier as the honesty check for systematic bias. That's basically your current design — and it argues *against* building the fancy faultfrac-uncertainty model. I was over-engineering; your "treat as hard data" instinct is the better call, with that one caveat noted.

Q2: What was the cross-incident correlation thing?

It's actually the *same* concern as the systematic-lean caveat above, which is why it's worth collapsing them. "Independent errors average out (√n)" only holds if Claude's mistakes are independent across incidents. If instead it systematically mis-rates a *class* of incident — e.g., consistently under-blames the AV on unprotected left turns — those errors point the same direction and compound instead of cancelling, no matter how many incidents you have. Correlated judgment error = a localized systematic bias. So Q2 isn't a separate thing to model; it's just the mechanism by which the bias risk in Q1 would show up. Same answer: the flip-multiplier bounds it; no separate model needed.

The trim only makes sense because of one thing that's easy to lose track of: we never measured Zoox's recent miles directly. We backed them out from the milestone.

Here's the logic in one line: the company says "~1M total by end of 2025." That's a fixed pie. When we built the recent series, we assumed Zoox drove ~0 before June 2025, so we sliced the *entire* ~1M pie into June–Dec 2025. Now we've learned an earlier slice exists (~250K, May 2024–May 2025). The pie is still ~1M. So the June–Dec slice has to shrink by ~250K to make room — that shrink *is* the trim.

It's just conservation: a fixed total can't gain a new chunk without losing an equal chunk somewhere else. We're moving ~250K of attribution from "recent" to "early," and the milestone caps the sum.

So the trim isn't a separate judgment — it's forced *if* you believe two things at once:

  1. the early miles are real (they are — same robotaxi), and
  2. they're counted inside the company's ~1M (plausible — same purpose-built fleet).

If both hold, then our old recent estimate was too high (it absorbed miles that were actually earned earlier), and trimming corrects it.

The additive option rejects #2. It says the early Foster City / SF-Explorer miles are *on top of* the company's "purpose-built robotaxi fleet" 1M — so the true total is ~1.25M, the company just wasn't counting the early stuff. Then nothing gets displaced, recent stays put, and our cumulative line sits ~25% above the company's stated figure.

That's the whole disagreement: is the ~1M the total (→ trim) or just the recent-fleet total (→ additive)? And the reason it barely matters is that the gap between those two interpretations is ~250K out of ~2.4M ≈ 10% on the recent window — inside the ±30% band we already carry. So the bell moves a hair either way.

For well-determined curves (Humans, Waymo, Tesla-at-fault) median = mode and the dot's on the peak; only the near-zero-data curves show the gap, and there it's honest.

Here's the factual answer, and it makes your instinct even better-founded than it looks. The default at-fault curves:

| helmer | k | MLE (V/k) | mean (V/(k−.5)) | mode-of-MPI | visual peak | median |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla | 5.75 | 352K | 386K | 280K | 330K | 342K |
| Waymo | 68 | 2.3M | 2.3M | 2.2M | 2.3M | 2.3M |
| Zoox | 0.1 | 20.2M | ∞ | 1.3M | 3.4M | 6.4M |

Three things fall out:

  1. No, none of {mean, median, mode} equals the MLE. They're genuinely four different points: MLE = V/k, mean = V/(k−½), mode-of-MPI = V/(k+1½), median = its own quantile. The MLE is the prior-free likelihood maximizer; the others are posterior summaries.
  1. The mean is the trap. For k ≤ 0.5 (Zoox at-fault, *every* zero-count metric) the posterior mean MPI is infinite — because there's real probability the at-fault rate is ~0, so "expected miles per incident" diverges. So "show all three" can't show the mean exactly on the curves where the spread is the whole story. (The MLE is also ∞ at k=0.)
  1. "Mode" is itself ambiguous — the mode of MPI (1.3M) ≠ the *visual* peak you see on the log axis (3.4M). They're different points.

So for a well-determined curve (Tesla, Waymo) all five values collapse to ~one point — one dot is honest. For a near-zero-data curve (Zoox) they fan from 1.3M to ∞ — and *that fanning is the message*: the point estimate is barely defined.

My recommendation: show two labeled dots — the visual peak ("most likely") and the median — both always finite and plottable; they coincide when the curve is well-determined and separate when it's skewed (the gap = the skew, self-documenting). The tooltip then lists the full breakdown — mode / median / mean / MLE, with "∞" shown where they diverge — so it's completely transparent which is which and *why* we don't lean on the mean/MLE. 19:43 Claude Code claude-opus-4-8 thought for 1m18s

Honest answer: no, not a clean one. #1 is a genuine tradeoff, not a Pareto improvement, which is exactly why it's been sitting unresolved.

The card CI and the fan bands are the double-extreme (vmtMin at the low rate tail, vmtMax at the high) — deliberately *wider* than the true marginal 95%. That same est.lo/est.hi drives the stress verdict, where the extra width is doing real anti-overclaim work: it makes both "robustly safer" *and* "robustly worse" harder to declare. Unifying on the marginal would:

  • (+) make the bell, the card CI, and the "95% CI" label all consistent and literally correct;
  • (−) narrow those intervals, so the verdict declares safer/worse more readily — a regression on the skeptical axis we intentionally chose.

So it's strictly better on consistency/honesty, strictly worse on conservatism. Not Pareto.

The only way to get *close* to Pareto is to decouple display from verdict — show the true marginal 95% on the cards/bell (consistent + honestly labeled), keep the conservative envelope for the verdict only. But that adds a second uncertainty concept (more code, two notions of "the interval"), so it's not free either — it trades simplicity.

Per the PDP, since there's no clean dominating move, I'd leave it unless you want to make the values call: consistency+honest-labels vs conservatism+simplicity. My weak lean is to leave it — the bell and the card CI live in different sections, so the inconsistency is latent, and the conservative verdict is a feature. Your call.

Where Waymo's 73.5M comes from

Waymo's page shows serious-or-fatal injury at 0.01 IPMM (rounded) vs a 0.23 benchmark, "94% fewer." Unrounded, "94% fewer than 0.23" ≈ 0.0136 IPMM, i.e. ~3 serious-or-fatal crashes over 220.6M miles → 220.6M / 3 ≈ 73.5M MPI. So your 73.5M is right (the rounded 0.01 would read as 100M; the real count is ~3).

Why we show ~40M

Full-history Waymo: 260.1M miles ÷ 6 "serious" incidents = 43.4M (≈40M after the Bayesian posterior-median shrinkage). We're counting ~2× more serious-injury events than Waymo does, for two reasons:

1. A genuine bug. The severity value "Serious" is *ranked* in SEVERITY_RANK (=5, between Moderate W/ Hospitalization=4 and Fatality=6) but is omitted from every classification set — INJURY_SEVERITIES, HOSPITALIZATION_SEVERITIES, and SERIOUS_INJURY_SEVERITIES ([crashla.js:749-766](crashla.js#L749-L766)). So the 3 Waymo "Serious" crashes (NOV-2023, OCT-2024, FEB-2025) silently fall through as no-injury in every metric — including, ironically, the serious-injury metric. They also undercount the plain *injury* metric (making Waymo look slightly *safer* there). It's an Anti-Postel hole: an unhandled severity vanishes instead of failing loudly.

2. A definitional mismatch. Our SSI+ bucket uses Moderate W/ Hospitalization + Fatality = 6. But "Moderate W/ Hospitalization" is a *moderate* injury that involved hospital transport (could be an ER visit) — broader than Waymo's KABCO-A "suspected serious injury." The literal Serious label is the on-the-nose KABCO-A match, and it's the one we drop.

| Definition | Count | Full-history MPI |
|---|--:|--:|
| Current (Moderate W/Hosp + Fatality) | 6 | 43.4M |
| KABCO A+K (Serious + Fatality) ✅ | 5 | 52.0M |
| Waymo's own (post-hoc determination) | ~3 | 73.5M |

Switching to the literal Serious + Fatality (= proper KABCO A+K) closes most of the gap to ~52M. The residual to 73.5M is expected and not a bug: SGO self-reported severity vs Waymo's careful post-hoc determination, all roads vs surface-streets-only, our denominator including the dense/immature pre-2023 miles, and Bayesian shrinkage on a small count.

  • Add a fail-loud assert + qual: every severity string present in the data must be classified by the injury sets (or explicitly listed as non-injury), so the next unhandled value crashes instead of disappearing.

The audit found the silent-drop class had three holes, not one — all in the hand-maintained severity sets:

The fix (root cause, not patch)

  • Single source of truth ([crashla.js](crashla.js)): one SEVERITY_INFO table with rank/injury/hosp/ssi/fatal flags per severity; INJURY_SEVERITIES, HOSPITALIZATION_SEVERITIES, SERIOUS_INJURY_SEVERITIES, and SEVERITY_RANK are now derived from it — they can't drift.
  • SSI+ redefined to KABCO A+K = {Serious, Fatality}; "Serious" added to injury+hosp+ssi; bare "Minor" added to injury; "Unknown" ranked.

Guards against the whole class (3 layers)

  1. Runtime assert — every incident's severity must be in SEVERITY_INFO or the app fails loudly at load.
  2. New qual ([quals/severity-classification.qual.mjs](quals/severity-classification.qual.mjs)) — coverage (every data severity classified), nesting (fatal⊆ssi⊆hosp⊆injury), rank-monotonicity (injury⟺rank≥1, ssi⟺rank≥5 — the invariant that directly catches this exact bug), plus Minor/Serious regression checks.
  3. Upstream Anti-Postel guard ([data/slurp.py](data/slurp.py)) — EXPECTED_SEVERITIES crashes the data build if NHTSA introduces a new severity string (verified complete against all snapshots).

The two fields legitimately measure *different things*: speed is the instantaneous speed at impact; svMovement is the pre-crash *maneuver category*. For "was the AV stationary when hit," speed == 0 is the right, authoritative signal, so the metric is already correct; there's nothing to mutate.

The standard way to handle two source fields that can disagree: (a) pick the authoritative one and document why, (b) don't mutate the source data, and (c) monitor the disagreement so a real regression surfaces loudly. Piper's article explicitly addresses this, citing Phil Koopman. The problem she identifies (with David Zipper's analysis):

humans were measured as *"vehicle miles traveled per death"* (a fleet metric — each death counted once, spread over all vehicles' miles), but Waymo was measured as *"miles per involvement with a fatal crash"* (a per-vehicle metric). Since "most fatal crashes have multiple vehicles involved," the per-vehicle metric "makes each car appear far more dangerous."

Koopman's fix, which Piper adopts: count a multi-vehicle fatal crash fractionally — *"count a two-car crash with one death as 0.5 deaths on Waymo's account."* She even gives Waymo's tally: *"0.33 in a three-vehicle crash… and 0.14 from a seven-car crash."*

That is exactly 1 / vehiclesInvolved. It's the adjustment that makes Waymo's count comparable to the fleet deaths-per-VMT human benchmark (FARS, ~1 death per 80M miles). Piper's own result — *Waymo ~0.5 fatalities over 127M mi vs ~1 per 80M → ~3× safer* — is precisely what the original code produced (~2.95×).

---

| Helmer | Median | 90% CI | Shape |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Waymo | ~4,700 | 3,300 – 6,750 | Lognormal (σ≈0.22) |
| Tesla | ~200 | 90 – 3,300 | Bimodal mixture (see below) |

---

Reasoning per helmer

Waymo — lognormal, median ≈ 4,700

Anchors: ~1,500 (May 2025) → ~2,500 (Nov 2025) → 3,067 (Dec 2025) → "~3,000" cited through Feb–May 2026; repo VMT uses ~3,000 cars for Apr–May 2026 (and VMT grew ~34% Dec→May, so effective capacity is rising even where the headcount reads flat). Growth drivers for H2 2026: the Mesa/Magna plant (tens of thousands/yr capacity), final Jaguar I‑PACE shipment + 2,000 more I‑PACE retrofits, new platforms (Zeekr RT 6th‑gen, Ioniq 5), a $16B Feb‑2026 round ($126B valuation), and 6+ new cities.

The honest tension: H1 2026 looks like a plateau near 3,000 while they wait on new platforms, against a clear, funded pipeline to add ~2,000+ vehicles. I center on resumed-but-not-explosive growth (~+50% over the year), with the band spanning "plateau persists" (~3,300) to "Mesa ramps hard" (~6,750). This is the tightest distribution of the three — Waymo's growth is supply-constrained and therefore relatively predictable.

Tesla — bimodal mixture, median ≈ 200 with a fat right tail

Anchors: TX fleet 25 (end‑Apr) → 42 registered (Jun 2), of which only ~20–25 are *active unsupervised*; repo notes ~58 total active TX incl. driver‑monitor mode. Austin ~20, Dallas 3, Houston 6. Musk himself says robotaxi revenue is immaterial in 2026, material "next year." Reality has run ~25–40× below his "1,000 cars in a month" launch projection.

But Tesla is structurally different from the other two: it has no vehicle‑supply constraint. Millions of FSD‑capable Model Ys exist, plus ~85 Cybercabs already built at Giga Texas (ramping). The only gates are (1) Tesla's internal confidence to pull the safety monitor and (2) regulators. Musk targets unsupervised FSD to customers "probably Q4 2026." So the outcome is event‑driven, not a smooth curve — which is why I model it as a mixture, not a lognormal:

  • ~75% "slow ramp persists": lognormal, median ~160 (range ~65–400). Tesla keeps cautiously adding Model‑Y robotaxis across TX/new metros.
  • ~25% "unsupervised greenlight / flood": lognormal, median ~3,000 (range ~1,000–9,000). If Q4 unsupervised approval lands and Tesla enrolls existing Model Ys + Cybercabs, the fleet jumps into the thousands almost overnight.

That tail is what produces the huge gap between the 50th (200) and 90th (3,300) percentiles.

If you use the looser definition (count supervised Bay Area Model Ys as "fleet"): add roughly +150–350 across the board.

Zoox — lognormal, median ≈ 150

Anchors: ~50 robotaxis (Jan 2026) → expanding to ~100 across Las Vegas + SF (Mar 2026); redesigned production‑intent robotaxi unveiled Jun 24–25 2026, series production "later in 2026." Hayward factory capacity up to 100/week (10k/yr) when scaled. Amazon‑funded. Gated by the NHTSA Part 555 / FMVSS exemption (no steering wheel) for paid rides — "optimistic, coming months" — plus CA DMV/CPUC for SF/LA. Joining Uber in LV summer 2026.

So the floor is fairly firm (~100, already achieved + deep pockets), and the upside depends on whether the new vehicle's series production + the federal exemption both land in H2 2026. Central ~150, with a right tail to ~400 if production ramps.

---

Cross-checks & caveats

  • Prediction‑market check (from the repo's snapshot): Manifold "Tesla has more AVs providing ridehailing than Waymo by Jan 2 2027" sits at 23%, and "Tesla serves more fully autonomous rides than Waymo in 2026" at 10%. The gap is probably part market optimism on the Tesla "flip the switch" tail and part a looser vehicle definition (the market likely counts supervised cars). I left my numbers grounded in the ADS‑only scope rather than over‑fitting one thin market, but it's a reason to take Tesla's upper tail seriously, not dismiss it.
  • Biggest single uncertainty: the Tesla Q4 unsupervised‑FSD decision. It's a discrete regulatory/confidence event, not a growth rate — hence the bimodality.
  • Definitional fragility: "fleet size" reporting mixes registered vs. active vs. in‑service vehicles; ±20% noise on any point estimate just from that.
  • These are my forecasts, not anything the repo asserts — the repo tops out at May 2026 VMT and tracks no vehicle counts directly.

Reproducible spec: Waymo = Lognormal(median 4700, σ 0.22); Zoox = Lognormal(median 150, σ 0.45); Tesla = 0.75·Lognormal(median 160, σ 0.55) + 0.25·Lognormal(median 3000, σ 0.75).

Side question: teslafsdtracker disengagement details

Short answer: you can get the breakdown by *type*, but not a per-event detail feed.

  • It does categorize every disengagement: *Critical Safety* (avoid accident, ran a red/stop, wrong side of road, unsafe action), *Non-critical* (wrong lane, courtesy, merge), and *Interventions* (accelerator tap, scroll wheel, turn signal). The dashboards have a "Top Causations for Disengagements" chart plus filters by HW3/HW4, city vs highway, FSD version, and geography. That's the closest thing to "what's causing the criticals."
  • It deliberately does not record routes — only distance traveled + the categorized event — so there's no per-event location or narrative, and no published per-event list, notes feed, or documented API/export.
  • It's crowdsourced and self-classified (submitted via the MATT3R K3Y extension, the EVGuyCanada in-car app, or manual entry validated by a VIN+firmware screenshot). So "critical" is whatever each submitter decided, with selection bias and small per-version samples — treat the rate as soft.

Ways to actually get more granularity:

  1. Run a logger yourself (EVGuyCanada / MATT3R) — your own drives give you event-level logs you control, just for your car.
  2. Ask the maintainer for raw submission data — it exists behind the aggregates; the Tesla Motors Club thread is the contact path.
  3. There's no official per-disengagement dataset for consumer FSD: NHTSA SGO only captures *crashes* (not disengagements), and California DMV disengagement reports only cover permitted AV *testing*, which Tesla's consumer FSD isn't filed under. So the crowdsourced tracker is essentially the only game in town.

Sources: teslafsdtracker help · Main dashboard · TMC discussion

Why the Waymo cumulative dot sits at the bottom of the band

It's not a rendering bug — it's how the cumulative ("kyoom") band is authored, and it's asymmetric by construction:

  • Lower bound (kyoom_min) is tightened up to Waymo's published cumulative milestones (127M, 170.7M, 220.6M…), which the methodology treats as floors — "Waymo has driven *at least* this much" (they under-state; e.g. "over 200M"). So kyoom_min ≈ the published number.
  • Upper bound (kyoom_max) was left as the running cumulative sum of the monthly +25–30% maxima — loose and compounding (~+28%). It was never re-tightened to the milestones.
  • The best-estimate dot is pinned to the milestone too (cume ≈ kyoom_min).

Net band ≈ [milestone, milestone×1.28] → tiny below, big above → dot at the bottom (I measured 1–26% up the band, and ~0–1% at the published-milestone months Sep'25 / Feb'26 / Mar'26).

This is documented (README: "published figures are encoded as lower-bound floors"), but there's a real inconsistency: the README also calls the Dec-2025 and Mar-2026 anchors "exact central estimates." If they're central, the +28% one-sided upper band around them is wrong — it should be roughly symmetric and tight there.

Recommended fix (F1), if you want it: tighten kyoom_max near the published anchors so the band is symmetric/tight at milestones and only bulges *between* them. It's a display-only edit to data/vmt.csv (kyoom feeds nothing but this chart — no MPI/safety number moves), and the kyoom-band qual still passes (kyoom_max stays ≥ cume and ≤ the running-sum). Yes — several real ones. I reviewed the newest code (the fleet forecast), cross-checked the data against Waymo's published milestones, and ran integrity checks over the incident data. Nothing changes the headline conclusions (default window unaffected in all cases), but three findings are substantive. Report only — I haven't changed anything.

Data errors

1. Early Waymo VMT contradicts Waymo's own published milestones — by up to 4x.
The series is anchored correctly from ~2024 onward but overshoots badly before that:

| Date | App cumulative | Published | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| end Jan 2023 | 4,217,018 | ~1M (crossed Jan 2023) | ~4.2x |
| end Oct 2023 | 9,813,999 | 7.14M (the 7.1M paper) | ~1.4x |
| end Jan 2025 | 59,374,000 | 56.7M (Kusano & Scanlon) | 1.05x |

The 2021–22 rows' own rationale *cites* the ~1M-Jan-2023 milestone, but the column sums to 3.67M by Dec 2022. Even the kyoom_min band (~2.1M at Jan 2023) excludes the true ~1M. This also explains an anomaly I found independently: 13 months in 2021–22 have VMT but zero Waymo incidents — 2.23M claimed miles that would predict ~15 incidents at the fleet's own overall rate (P(0) ≈ e⁻¹⁵). With VMT corrected ~4x down, expectation drops to ~4, which is merely unlucky rather than impossible. Impact: early points on the full-history MPI chart read ~4x too safe; window totals and the default view are unaffected since later months are anchor-pinned.

2. The Jan-2025 SF fatality has vehiclesInvolved = 2; its narrative describes six vehicles.
The narrative (report 30270-9724) lists the AV, the car behind it, the SUV, a fourth car, plus "at least two other vehicles" per SFPD, and "five passengers in four of the vehicles" injured. [slurp.py:130](data/slurp.py:130)'s own rule says to override the default of 2 "when the narrative reveals more vehicles were involved" — but VEHICLES_INVOLVED contains only the Sep-2025 Tempe fatality (set to 3). Under the Koopman fractional-death method this death should count ~1/6 on Waymo's account, not 1/2: full-history Waymo fatality mass 0.833 → 0.5, i.e. fatality MPI currently understated ~1.67x. The error is in the anti-Waymo (conservative) direction, and the default window is unaffected (JAN-2025 is outside it). Note the 2026-06-27 review entry assumed both fatalities had explicit overrides; only one does.

3. Waymo cumulative rides history sits below published milestones — outside its own bands.
RIDES_HISTORY.Waymo has 7M [6M–8.5M] at Jun 2025, but Waymo announced 10M cumulative paid trips on May 20, 2025; and 17M [14M–21M] at Dec 2025 vs ~20M lifetime by end of 2025. The section self-describes as "loosely sourced" from weekly rates, but these cumulative milestones were headline announcements and fall outside the authored 90% bands. The Jan-2027 forecast (48M) is roughly consistent with the *true* trajectory, so the drawn dashed extrapolation has the wrong slope rather than the wrong endpoint.

4. First-month kyoom band incoherence (introduced in the Forecast graphs commit).

#7 (weight fit): keep it as-is. The documented assumption — scenario C implies the market resolves YES — is the more defensible reading. If Tesla flips eyes-off across ~hundreds of thousands of HW4 cars, the market's "vehicles providing ridehailing" threshold (~6k, Waymo's fleet) is cleared by even ~1% owner participation in Tesla Network, and a C-world also unthrottles Tesla's first-party robotaxi fleet, since the binding constraint (software validation) is gone by hypothesis. So P(YES | C) is ~0.9–1, not 0, and the arithmetic barely moves: 0.24×0.73 + 0.05×0.95 ≈ 0.22 ≈ the market. Bumping B to 0.32 would distort the robotaxi-scope curve on the strength of the *less* plausible reading.

#5 (forecast best): the current fix is consistent but I'd go one step further — model Tesla's miles/rides as the scenario mixture, like the fleet metric already does. Here's the actual problem: your belief about Tesla's Jan-2027 miles isn't a one-humped distribution. It's the push-forward of the A/B/C scenarios — ~71% "boring, ~8M", ~24% "aggressive, tens of millions", ~5% "HW4, hundreds of millions". The two-piece log-normal can't represent that, and it distorts the median in a specific way: it smears the 29% non-A mass into one huge fat tail, which drags the computed median out to ~32M. Under the true mixture, the median would sit just above the A-scenario — probably ~9–12M, close to your authored 8M. So neither the old display (8M labeled "Median", 14th percentile of the drawn curve) nor the current one (~32M, honest for the drawn curve but the drawn curve misrepresents the belief) is really right; the *density* is the thing to fix.

The upgrade is cheap and makes the three metrics uniform: give Tesla's miles and rides the same mixture structure as FLEET_FORECAST — reuse the A/B/C weights (0.71/0.24/0.05) with per-scenario miles/rides log-normals, and split the display into the same two lanes (robotaxi-scope solid = A+B, HW4-scope dashed conditional = C). That also fixes a scope inconsistency for free: right now the 500M hi bakes C's personal-car miles into Tesla's *single* miles curve, while the fleet chart carefully quarantines C into a dashed conditional lane. All the machinery exists (fleetMixtureLogDensity/Quantiles, the lane splitter); what's needed from you is per-scenario medians, though they can be derived mechanically — e.g. miles ≈ current 3.4M cumulative + fleet-scenario trajectory × miles-per-vehicle-month calibrated from today's fleet (~40–60 vehicles doing ~430k mi/mo → ~8–10k mi/vehicle-month), giving roughly A ≈ 7.5M, B ≈ 20–30M, C ≈ 300–600M.

The anchor chain

Tesla's own quarterly disclosures of cumulative paid Robotaxi miles (a strict subset of the repo's total-scope driverless VMT, which adds deadhead/unpaid miles):

| Date | Tesla-disclosed paid cume | Repo total-scope cume |
|---|---|---|
| 2025-10-22 (Q3 call) | ~250k "total miles" | ~250k (anchor) |
| 2025-12-31 (Q4 deck) | 610k | 650k (robotaxitracker anchor) |
| ~2026-02-15 (Q4-call-era reporting) | ~700k | ~800k interpolated |
| 2026-03-31 (Q1 deck) | 1.7M | 1,563,047 |

The decisive datapoint: Tesla's Q1-2026 shareholder update says paid Robotaxi miles reached 1.7M by end of Q1, up from 610k at end of Q4 2025 (Drive Tesla, quoting the deck directly). Scope is the Texas driverless network — the deck frames it as unsupervised Austin plus the April Dallas/Houston launch, and the repo's README already documents (from the Q3-2025 call transcript) that Bay Area safety-driver miles are excluded from Tesla's Robotaxi metric. So it's apples-to-apples with the repo's scope, and it's a *floor* (paid miles exclude deadhead). Cumulative in-scope VMT was ≥1.7M nearly four months ago; April–June added Dallas/Houston plus continued Austin service. ~1M cumulative today can't be reconciled with Tesla's own numbers.

Where ~1M likely came from

The most plausible reconstruction: spotted-active-fleet × the trackers' "115 mi/vehicle/day" heuristic. Roughly 25–35 average active vehicles × 115 mi/day × ~13 months lands right at 1.1–1.6M. Your own project notes (memory, 2026-07-15) explicitly warn against exactly this: only the fleet×utilization *product* is anchored, spotted counts are a floor, and this method undershoots the hard-anchored Oct→Dec 2025 window by ~2x. Alternative origins — extrapolating from the stale 610–650k end-2025 anchor, or the ~700k paid figure from February — land in the same place.

  1. The Q1-2026 rows are below the paid-only floor. The Q1 rationale reads Tesla's "paid robotaxi miles ~doubled sequentially" as "Q1 ≈ 2x Q4," giving a Q1 delta of 913k. Yes — and it's deliberate, not an accident. Here's the picture:

The row. [vmt.csv](data/vmt.csv) Tesla 2026-07: best 170k, band [55k, 340k] = 0.32×–2.0×. Every deck-anchored month before it is 0.85×–1.25× (Feb 324k … Jun 157k). So July is ~4× wider than its neighbors.

Why. July is the first "extension month" past Tesla's last hard anchor. The only real Tesla VMT source is the "Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles" chart in the quarterly deck; the Q2 deck pinned 2.440M cumulative at end-June, and the next anchor is the Q3 deck (~late Oct). In between, the number is extrapolation, and the extrapolation method has a bad recent track record: the pre-pin activity-ratio estimates for Q2 ran ~28% high (June rationale), and the earlier fleet-count ratios ran ~2× hot — a utilization-led slowdown the fleet counts didn't see. So the July row is explicitly a placeholder: best held near the May–Jun run-rate (170k), floor = taking robotaxitracker's late-July "approaching 2.5M" literally (2.5M − 2.44M ≈ 55k for the month), ceiling = ~2× June's pace on the new-metro upside (Miami driverless Jul 3, Tampa/Orlando Jul 21). The Aug 10 source survey found nothing to tighten it.

Whether it's *too* wide. Arguments it's about right:

  • The floor is a real datapoint in the same scope, not a hedge — if the tracker's cumulative is right, July really was ~60k and 170k is a 3× overestimate.
  • The ceiling is the mirror: six metros vs. three, if the fleet actually ramps.
  • It's monthly, and July is also at 11% incident coverage, so the July point on the chart is dominated by *both* uncertainties anyway.
  • Effect on the cumulative-based Tesla numbers is modest: kyoom band goes from [2.37M, 2.81M] at end-June (−3%/+15%) to [2.42M, 3.15M] (−7%/+21%) — July adds roughly ±140k on a 2.6M base.

Argument it's too generous on the *upside*: 340k would be Tesla's second-best month ever (only Mar 438k beats it) at a time when the unsupervised fleet has stalled at ~17–21 cars and utilization was already falling; 1.5× June (~235k) is arguably a fairer ceiling. The downside floor I'd leave alone.

When it resolves. Same as May/June did: the Q3 deck (~late Oct) pins Jul–Sep and the band snaps back to 0.85×–1.25×. Until then it's honest about how little is known.

1. Yes — robotaxitracker stopped estimating VMT. Wayback shows the history. Jan 9: extrapolation model. Jan 31: linear anchor interpolation. The model, widget, and every mileage string are gone. The live methodology page lists only: vehicle registry, rider-logged trips/receipts, wait times, first-spotted dates, government data. Its "miles" now means contributor trip miles: 10,499 mi over 2,922 trips as of Aug 8.

Two details matter for us. The old model's anchors were only 7k / 250k / 650k (Jul–Dec 2025). It never took the Q1 (1.717M) or Q2 (2.44M) deck points. Its nowcast value was client-rendered from an API Wayback never captured. So a late-July reading is unrecoverable, and it would have been a Dec-2025-anchored fleet extrapolation anyway. That method ran 2× hot in Q2. The July floor is not a datapoint under either reading. My rationale-fix recommendation stands, with this added to it.

It means "derived by tilting the AV-cities band" — a coinage, not standard English.

The mechanics are in [crashla.js:519-527](crashla.js#L519-L527). For every metric except fatality, the Humans (Uber/Lyft) band is built from the Humans (AV cities) band rather than sourced independently:

  • lo = AV.lo ÷ 1.2 — rideshare drivers might crash up to 1.2× more often (lower MPI = worse)

The pixelation

Replicata. Load at devicePixelRatio 2, zoom in on the top-left corner of the abstract or any heading rule.
Expectata. A drawn line, antialiased like the text beside it.
Resultata. The stroke is chopped into hard-edged segments sitting at whole-pixel offsets, with *no partial coverage on the steps*, and notches bitten out of the vertical edge.

Cause: feDisplacementMap. It resamples the source nearest-neighbour and offsets by whole *device* pixels. On a 2.5px stroke each wobble is a jog of ~40% of the stroke width landing with zero antialiasing. Not a browser bug — Chromium, Firefox and WebKit (all three launched from the playwright cache) produce it identically.

Three plausible explanations were tested and ruled out, rather than assumed:

  1. Not 1×-rasterize-then-upscale. Edge-run lengths aren't quantized to DPR (23% at 3×, 60% at 2× — about chance) and half the edge-band pixels are midtones. The filter does run at device resolution.
  2. Not gamma. SVG filters default to linearRGB, a classic crunchy-edge culprit. Adding color-interpolation-filters="sRGB" gave a pixel-identical result.
  3. Not filter-region size. The abstract (253px tall) and the market list (946px) were equally chewed.

Tuning helps but can't cure it: one octave, baseFrequency .04 → .012, and a blurred displacement field make the steps longer and fewer, never softer, because the offset stays an integer.

Fix. All three <filter> defs deleted; every filter: url() gone. index.html is now back to net-zero diff. The heading and footer rules are a 198px hand-drawn wave in a data-URI SVG used as a mask-image over background: var(--line) — shape in the token, color in the palette, path antialiased properly, and it starts and ends at y=4.3 with matching slope so repeat-x has no seam. The abstract and market list dropped their border-drawing ::before and carry a plain 2.5px border; the wobble was always coming from border-radius, which never aliased. Verified smooth at 9× in all three engines — that comparison is the figure in the artifact.

Links

--accent back to #2060c0.

That change surfaced a defect the first pass introduced: warming --wash to #f6f2ea had quietly dropped --iffy to 4.31:1 on it, and .pm-subcard paints .pm-card-odds.mid there. Nudged to #806716. It was caught by a new qual that computes WCAG contrast for every meaning-bearing token against --paper/--card/--wash, not by eye. (--ink-faint is deliberately excluded — it's the de-emphasized meta text and has always been sub-AA, before this work too.)

Qual spec change — flagging per rule 5

sketch-style.qual.mjs §4 previously asserted the displacement filters exist. It now asserts the opposite: no feDisplacementMap in index.html, no filter: url() in style.css, and that --drawn-rule is an SVG path used through mask-image with the -webkit- prefix over a tokenized background. §5 (no filter on a layout ancestor) is kept as a hazard guard. The quals were one turn old and mine rather than yours, but the technique they encoded turned out to be the bug, so the reversal is worth naming.

Good question to push on — here's the honest anatomy:

How it was wrong

A press floor got treated as a central. The old series was pinned to "~1M autonomous miles by late 2025," which came from press coverage (Electrek et al.). But the press phrasing was "*over* 1 million" — a floor — and the curve pinned end-Dec at 1.001M, i.e. the floor read as the level. The truth, 1.3M, satisfies "over 1M" perfectly well. (Same error-class as two other things this audit caught: the Waymo milestone-minus-150k inconsistency and Tesla's "approaching 2.5M" circular floor. Floors and centrals kept getting conflated.)

Structurally, Zoox is the blind helmer. Tesla publishes a deck chart; Waymo publishes cumulative rider-miles plus CPUC actuals covering ~50% of its miles. Zoox publishes almost nothing on a schedule — CPUC covers only ~20% of its miles (32–68k/mo of ~200–300k), and CA DMV data is drivered-dominated. So the series was press-milestone interpolation, which is why it carried 0.7×–1.3× bands — and to the credit of that honesty, the authored band did contain 1.3M (kyoom max was 1.337M; 2.8% headroom). The central was 30% low; the stated uncertainty just barely covered the miss.

Why nobody caught it earlier: the correcting document is buried in a regulations.gov docket attachment (Zoox's Jan 28, 2026 letter answering NHTSA's questions on the FMVSS exemption petition). Your 20-agent and 82-agent source sweeps found the *press* milestones and the Aug-6 "3M+" announcement but never surfaced the docket PDF — it has zero mentions anywhere in the repo pre-Codex. Credit where due: that was Codex's single best find.

How sure are we now?

High confidence on the anchors:

  • The 1.3M is Zoox's own statement to its federal regulator, in a Part 555 exemption proceeding — about the strongest provenance class available, and both my verifier and its adversarial challenger *independently* downloaded the PDF and read p.22 Q21a verbatim, confirming the scope in-document (robotaxi-only, driverless, public-road; the drivered Highlander test fleet itemized separately — so it matches our series' scope).
  • The three anchors mutually corroborate: 1.3M (Dec 31) → ~2M (late Mar) → >3M (Aug 6) implies a smooth ~230–260k/mo ramp with no gymnastics. And end-July stayed at 3,051,000, within ~2% of the Aug-6 official figure.
  • CPUC CA actuals stay consistent as the minor share throughout.
  • The provenance qual now pins all three milestones — it went red at 0.770 on the old data, green on the new, and any future official disclosure that contradicts the curve trips it.

Where uncertainty honestly remains (and the 0.7–1.3× bands stay wide because of it):

  1. Monthly allocation between anchors is still authored — the anchors nail Dec/Mar/Jul cumulatives; the month-by-month shape is interpolation (I preserved the old ramp's shape, scaled ×1.36).
  2. The pre-Jun-2025 segment (178k) is still near-blind — the docket's by-year mileage table is redacted in the public PDF, so the 1.3M can't be split by year. If early miles were really bigger, late-2025 months shrink correspondingly.
  3. Wording drift across sources: "driverless autonomous miles on public roads" (docket) vs "autonomous miles" (~2M press) vs "miles on public roads" (Aug 3M+) — the middle anchor is the softest. All are within the qual's 15% slack convention.

Net effect on conclusions: small — the default-window Zoox total is byte-identical (2,873,000), only its within-window distribution moved, and no Zoox verdict changed. The headline correction is really about the *full-history* denominator and about the curve now resting on an official disclosure instead of a misread press floor.

The ChatGPT conversation is a 13-item audit of the deployed site.   1. Coverage applied uniformly across severities — the one real modeling bug (audit #6). One pooled incident_coverage (~10.7% for July 2026) was thinning effective VMT for *every* metric. Why "no change" is recommended, in full:

  1. What the band has to bracket. The AV side counts each incident at P(expert human in the AV's seat would have avoided it), so its rate is "expert-avoidable involvements per mile." The matching human quantity is the human crash-involvement rate × s, where s = share of human involvements an expert would have avoided. Human at-fault MPI = all-crash MPI / s. The band edges are (all-crash lo, s_hi) and (all-crash hi, s_lo): atfault uses s ∈ [0.5, ~1], atfaultInjury s ∈ [0.5, 0.94].
  1. The ordering ChatGPT says doesn't exist does exist, approximately. Expert-avoidable ⊇ legally-at-fault, minus rare exceptions (sudden medical event, mechanical failure — legally the driver's, unavoidable for an expert). An expert avoids nearly everything you'd be liable for, plus some crashes you weren't liable for (defensive driving — exactly what the faultfrac calibration anchors give partial credit for: 0.15–0.4 on other-party violations). So s ≥ legal-fault share holds to within a few percent. Per involvement, legal-fault share ≈ single-vehicle share + ½·multi-vehicle share ≈ 0.32 + 0.68×0.5 ≈ 0.66 (CRSS: ~32% of crashes are single-vehicle). A floor of 0.5 is therefore conservative by a margin, in the direction that hurts the AVs.
  1. The floor is doing real work. With the coverage fix, Zoox at-fault is ambiguous at ratio 0.80x (AV lo 344k / human hi 430k). At s = 0.66 the human hi edge would be 324k and Zoox would flip to "safer" on k=2. The 0.5 edge is what keeps that verdict honest. Waymo (3.07x at the same edge) and Tesla (0.43x) are nowhere near a flip.
  1. The 94% edge only affects the AV-favorable end, which no robust verdict uses. NHTSA 812115: driver-attributed critical reason in 94% ±2.2% of NMVCCS crashes (EMS-dispatched + tow-away sample, closer to injury crashes than to PDO contacts). NHTSA's disclaimer says critical reason ≠ cause ≠ fault — correct, and irrelevant to how it's used here: as an upper bound on what an expert could avoid (an expert can't do much better than avoiding every crash where some human erred, plus a slice of the 6% vehicle/environment ones). Per-involvement the true s_hi is probably lower (~0.7–0.8, since the non-erring driver in a two-car crash only sometimes avoids it), which would *raise* the human lo edge and shrink the AV-favorable end of the band — a band-tightening, not a threat to any verdict. Swapping 0.94 for 1.0 (what atfault already uses) moves atfaultInjury lo 147k→138k, 6% on a 6.7x-wide band.
  1. Point estimate sits well inside. s ≈ 0.65–0.8 by either route (legal share + defensive credit, or per-involvement critical-reason accounting) → human at-fault MPI ≈ 270k–330k inside [103k, 430k]. The band is 4.2x wide (atfault) and 6.7x (atfaultInjury); a band that already spans the plausible range on both sides, with its verdict-relevant edge on the conservative side, is what "wide error bars where the data is poor" means.
  1. What would actually be more exact, if anything: the src wording. "94% expert-avoidability share (NHTSA critical reason)" labels a critical-reason statistic as an avoidability share; the precise statement is "94% = crashes with a driver-attributed critical reason, taken as an upper bound on expert avoidability." That's a rule-7 Latin edit to one src string plus its HumansUS twin — a precision fix, no numbers move. Not recommended over the numbers because the numbers aren't wrong; the label is loose.

How we "know" paid miles include deadhead. Tesla has never defined "Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles." The reading was settled on 2026-07-22 (ledger entry at [AGENTS.md:92](AGENTS.md#L92)) on three converging pieces of evidence, plus a hedge for being wrong:

  2. The trackers equate the disclosures to fleet-wide miles. robotaxitracker's old methodology and robotaxi-safety-tracker both anchored on Tesla's ~115 miles per vehicle per day fleet-wide disclosure with no split by occupancy. Their nowcasts matched Tesla's cumulative figures only under the fleet-miles reading.
  3. Per-vehicle throughput math agrees. Dividing the disclosed cumulative by the active fleet and service days gives plausible fleet-service mileage. A literal passenger-aboard-only reading would require implausibly high utilization for a fleet that size.
  4. The hedge is asymmetric on purpose. If "paid" is literal and excludes deadhead, the true fleet mileage is higher, never lower. So the chart-month kyoom bands are set at roughly 0.97c to 1.15c rather than symmetric. The rides corridor separately encodes deadhead via the 0.6 to 0.85 on-trip share at [crashla.js:2552](crashla.js#L2552).

The one known tension, noted in the same ledger entry: the Oct 2025 call's "more than a quarter million" runs about 10% above the chart-interpolated value for that date. The chart wins because it is the series we can extract month by month.

Tesla's August VMT

It is an inference from two Tesla statements, not a measured figure. No source reports August miles directly.

The two disclosures bracket the window. Elluswamy said "more than 380,000" unsupervised miles on the July 22 earnings call, and "1 million miles of unsupervised Robotaxi operation" at the September 3 Cybercab event. That is 620,000 miles over 43 days, about 14,400 per day.

The jump is forced by those numbers, not chosen. June's measured rate from the Q2 deck was 5,233 miles per day. At that rate the fleet covers 225,000 miles in 43 days, not 620,000. So the reversal of the April-to-June decline is Tesla's own arithmetic.

The allocation across the window is where the judgment enters. A flat split gives August 447,000; the row carries 470,000 with a band of 360,000 to 600,000.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Flat allocation, August share | 447,000 |
| If "more than 380k" means 420k | 418,000 |
| If "1 million" means 1.1M | 519,000 |
| Miles per vehicle per day at 173 vehicles | 88 |
| Same at Electrek's "~20 active" | 758 |

Every sensitivity lands inside the authored band, and 88 miles per vehicle per day is plausible for 6am-to-10pm service. The 758 figure is why Electrek's active-fleet claim was rejected.

One structural point in your favor: unsupervised miles are a subset of the service miles the denominator counts, so 620,000 is a floor, not a midpoint. If monitors were still aboard for part of August, the true total is higher.

The weak links are the allocation shape and the fact that both endpoints are round, loose statements. The Q3 deck around October 21 to 28 is the next hard anchor.

No Tesla incidents in August

Confirmed: zero Tesla rows carry an August 2026 incident date, under any operator type. Zoox is also zero. The only August incidents are 10 Waymo, all on the five-day track.

That zero is the expected outcome, not a safety signal. Probability of observing zero is about 86%. Two filters multiply:

  • Tesla files almost everything on the Monthly track. Only 2 of its 16 incidents in 2026 ever carried a five-day filing, about 12%. Monthly reports for August were not due until September 15, so they arrive in the October release.
  • Only about 28% of a month's five-day filings are received by the cutoff.

So expected visible Tesla August incidents are 4.4 × 0.12 × 0.28, which is 0.15. Even using Waymo's much higher 46% five-day share, the expectation is 0.57 and seeing zero still runs about 57%.

The caveat: that 12% rests on 16 incidents, so it is noisy. But the conclusion holds across the range.

Worth stating plainly, since it is the failure mode you would care about: the model does not treat those 470,000 miles as incident-free exposure. The August row carries receipt coverage 0.28 and pooled incident coverage 0.3313, which discount the exposure to match the reporting frontier. The real test of the August mileage comes in the October release, when Tesla's Monthly filings land and the receipt-coverage assumption gets checked against actual counts.

But the answer to your second question got stronger, not weaker, because the empirical record beats my reasoning:

| Release | Data-through month | Waymo shown | Tesla shown |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apr-15 | 2026-03 | 24 | 0 |
| May-15 | 2026-04 | 2 | 0 |
| Jun-15 | 2026-05 | 15 | 0 |
| Jul-15 | 2026-06 | 16 | 1 |
| Aug-17 | 2026-07 | 11 | 0 |
| Sep-15 | 2026-08 | 10 | 0 |

Tesla shows zero in the data-through month in five of the last six releases. July is the direct precedent: zero in the August release, two now. So yes, I am confident there are no Tesla August incidents in this release, and I expect two to four of them to appear in the October one.

I also tested the thing that would actually hurt us. If Tesla is reliably absent from the data-through month while the model still credits it 470,000 miles discounted by a coverage factor derived mostly from Waymo, Tesla would get exposure that cannot produce incidents, flattering its safety every release. That worry does not survive the data: across the six data-through months Tesla shows 1 incident against 1.98 expected, which gives p = 0.41. No detectable bias. The documented pooling choice holds up.

On the mileage, nothing I found changes it, and I want to be precise about what "sure" means. The floor is solid: Tesla's own two statements force at least 620,000 unsupervised miles between July 22 and September 3, which cannot be reconciled with June's measured rate. The split of that total into a specific August number is a modeling choice, which is what the 360,000 to 600,000 band is for.

The one assumption still carrying real weight is that the September 3 "1 million" and the July 22 "380,000" are the same series. I verified that across Electrek, Teslarati and AP on September 7, and both are Elluswamy describing unsupervised robotaxi operation. If that were wrong, say if the million quietly included the Bay Area supervised miles, August would be too high. The Q3 deck around October 21 settles it.

| Base gap: 0.7rem | 1 | 27px |

My recommendation is column-gap: 1rem; row-gap: 0.7rem. Simply deleting the override also works, but someone presumably raised it to 1.5rem for a reason: each item's internal gap between checkbox, chip and label is 0.35rem, so the space *between* items has to read as clearly larger or the grouping inverts. 1rem keeps that roughly 3-to-1 separation, fits on one line with 11px of slack, and still tightens the vertical gap for narrow windows where wrapping is unavoidable.

No. None of the crashes I proposed adding were remote-operated; the software was driving in all four, and another party caused each one. Here's how the pieces fit.

What "Remote" means in NHTSA's field. It says a remote operator was involved, not that one was driving. Both reports I proposed adding say the software was driving: the filings mark it "Verified Engaged", and the narratives say "Level 4 ADS was engaged in autonomous mode" (Waymo) and "unoccupied Zoox autonomous vehicle" (Zoox). Both cars were stopped or slowing when a cyclist ran a red light into one and a car rear-ended the other. They're driverless-service crashes our filter currently drops only because of how the operator field is coded.

Our metrics come in two kinds, and that decides what "counts against" means:

  • At-fault metrics (the default view): each crash is weighted by how avoidable it was for the software. A crash a remote human caused scores 0, so it never counts against the helmer. Tesla's Houston tree stump, the one genuinely remote-driven crash in the data, is already scored 0. This is the direct measure of the software.
  • Involvement metrics (all incidents, injury, airbag, and so on): every crash the car was in counts, whoever caused it, because the human benchmarks they're compared against count every crash humans are in. A Waymo rear-ended at a red light counts here too. So these four would count the same way the hundreds of hit-while-stopped crashes already do.

Safety-driver crashes. Whether they count is decided by which miles are in each company's denominator, not by who's in the seat.

  • Waymo and Zoox: our miles are driverless miles only, so safety-driver crashes have to stay out whether or not the software was engaged. Counting them without their miles would inflate the crash rate.
  • Tesla: its published miles mix in monitor-aboard miles and can't be split, so those crashes have to stay in. All three Tesla safety-monitor crashes are marked "Verified Engaged", so the software was driving each time.

The remaining distortion is crashes a monitor might have prevented. That makes Tesla look better than its software, can't be corrected, and fades now that Austin runs without monitors.

On engagement: older reports (before mid-2025) don't carry the engaged field at all. In the current data, 3 counted Waymo crashes are marked "Alleged Engaged" or "Verified Not Engaged". In all three the car was stopped or parked and got hit, and each narrative says the software was engaged.

The 7 areas:

  1. NHTSA's reporting rules for Level 2 crashes.
  2. Recounting the Level 2 file.
  3. Mileage figures that could serve as denominators.
  4. Tesla's own FSD safety statistics.
  5. NHTSA investigations into FSD.
