The Level 2 file says almost nothing about how safe FSD would be unsupervised. The one source that does bear on it is the robotaxi data the app already uses. This comes from a 24-agent research run, with the load-bearing facts re-checked against the primary sources.

Why the Level 2 reports can't answer it

  1. A human supervised every mile. Crashes FSD would have caused but the driver prevented never happen, so they're never reported. At best, supervised crash counts put a floor under the unsupervised rate. Even that floor leaks: a crash counts as "engaged" if FSD was on within 30 s, including when the driver overrode it. Example: the fatal Katy, TX crash of Jun 19, 2026. FSD was engaged, the driver floored the accelerator, and the car hit a house at over 70 mph on a 30-mph street (NTSB).
  2. Only severe crashes qualify. Since Jun 16, 2025 a Level 2 crash is reportable only for a death, a hospital transport, a struck pedestrian/cyclist/motorcyclist, or an airbag deployment on any vehicle (Third Amended SGO, Request 1.D). Tow-aways and minor damage count only for driverless vehicles. Applied to the 23 robotaxi incidents, that filter keeps 2, both at fault 0.
  3. Everything is redacted and there's no mileage.
  • All 1,943 Tesla Level 2 reports withhold the narrative, software version and operating-domain field, so FSD can't be told apart from Autopilot.
  • The 23 commercial/test reports mix four things: Bay Area ride-hail with a safety driver, pre-launch validation cars (Bedford TX, Tampa, Miami), test cars, and 4 Austin cars of unknown program.
  • Only 5 involve the Tesla's front or reversing. Five are cyclists (or similar) passing a stopped Tesla in SF, which looks like passengers dooring them.
  • The only Bay Area figures: ">1 million miles" by Oct 2025, including manual driving. Tesla told the CPUC it had "reported only three events" over >40,000 rides (filing).
  1. The consumer reports mostly count Tesla airbag deployments. 98% record the Tesla's own airbag deploying, and 93% arrived by telematics. Only 5 of the 837 with a known crash partner hit a pedestrian, cyclist or motorcyclist, versus ~7% for humans at the same threshold. Monthly counts tripled, but reports per FSD mile stayed flat at ~0.2 per million: more driving, not worse driving.

What the floor shows

Tesla's own data (safety report) counts airbag/pretensioner crashes per million miles off highways:

  • supervised FSD: 0.28
  • Teslas driven manually: 0.64
  • humans, own airbag, off interstates (NHTSA's 2024 crash sample): ~0.72

So FSD plus an attentive driver looks good. But a floor below the human rate rules nothing out, and nothing public supplies a ceiling.

What does bear on unsupervised FSD

  1. The robotaxi. It runs the FSD stack ("early versions of the v15 FSD software", per the Q2 call).
  • The app rates it ambiguous on all incidents and on at-fault.
  • It had 0 airbag crashes in ~2.68M miles. Austin human rates predict 4.8–6.2 (p ≈ 0.002–0.008); national surface-street rates predict ~2.5; Waymo's own Austin rate predicts 0.6.
  • Caveats: ~84% of those miles had a monitor aboard, Travis County's airbag benchmark looks inflated by local crash coding, and 1M monitor-free miles alone bound the rate only at ≤3.0 per million.
  1. Interventions.
  • Enthusiast v14 logs (FSD Community Tracker, 34 testers) show one self-labeled critical takeover per ~1,800 miles.
  • To match humans on airbag crashes, fewer than ~1 in 2,000 of those takeovers (range 1 in 800 to 1 in 3,600) could have been would-be airbag crashes.
  • Tesla says it simulates exactly this and publishes nothing.
  • The closest stand-ins (near-crash-to-crash ratios from naturalistic driving studies, Waymo's counterfactual simulations) span ~2× better to ~6× worse than the human crash rate. Low confidence.
  1. NHTSA probes show failure modes but give no rates.
  • EA26002: FSD flagged blinded cameras only "immediately before" reduced-visibility crashes, one of which killed a pedestrian.
  • PE25012: red-light entries, six crashes, all before v14.

Bottom line: how safe unsupervised consumer FSD would be relative to humans is unknown, and public data can't resolve it. The deciding number, how many takeovers were would-be crashes, is unpublished. Tesla also asked NHTSA to keep its mileage-by-mode answers confidential in all three probes. The robotaxi is the only real test so far: ambiguous to favorable, on small numbers, in a protected setting.

The spread of Waymo multipliers is expected

Waymo's own hub data, split by crash type (all locations, through June 2026), shows the same spread:

| Crash type | Police-reported | Injury |
|---|---|---|
| Single vehicle | 19x | 36x |
| Intersection | 9.1x | 27x |
| Pedestrian | 13x | 13x |
| Cyclist | 7.7x | 7.2x |
| Sideswipe | 3.1x | 5.7x |
| Rear-end | 2.4x | 1.9x |
| Secondary | 1.6x | 2.4x |
| Head-on | 1.0x | 2.0x |
| Backing | 0.6x | 1.4x |
| All crashes | 3.9x | 5.6x |

The top rows are crashes a driver usually causes. The bottom rows are crashes where the Waymo is mostly the one struck:

  • Rear-ends: the Waymo was stopped in 71 of its 127 police-reported ones, and 96% have fault 0.
  • Backing: the one type where Waymo does worse than humans. The Waymo was stopped or parked in 30 of 39 and was itself reversing in only 2.

Every overall multiplier mixes these two groups. Metrics dominated by being struck sit at 1–3x; at-fault and severe outcomes sit at 10–20x or more. The severe ones are dominated by speeding, red-light and single-vehicle crashes, which Waymo rarely causes. The site's 11x at-fault against 1.2x all-incidents is exactly that pattern.

The genuinely odd values come from site-specific choices:

  • Fatality, 2.3x. It rests on 0.8 fractional deaths.

The three gaps, all traced to definitions:

  2. Airbag. The site's multiplier is 17% higher because of where it centers the human benchmark.
  3. All incidents. Every reported contact vs police-reported crashes only.

What can't be checked: Waymo's per-crash police determinations are internal, and the hub publishes nothing on fault. So the at-fault metrics have no Waymo counterpart beyond the 2024 Swiss Re claims study.

That macOS dialog usually means some process tried to read another app's private data folder, and Claude Code's subprocesses count as VS Code. So the likely source is one of the audit's agents. Checking their recent commands.

Checking which Claude Code tool call set off the macOS prompt. The log shows Claude Code's own process did the access, not VS Code.

Found it. Saving a note so future agent prompts keep searches inside the project folders.

The dialog came from one of the audit agents. At 12:15:04 the links-and-citations agent ran find / -name "CRSS2024CSV*" -maxdepth 8, which searches the whole disk for the CRSS 2024 data files. Because it started at /, it walked into other apps' private data folders under ~/Library, and macOS asks before any program looks inside those.

The dialog names VS Code because Claude Code swaps the usual find and grep commands for copies built into its own program. macOS's privacy log at 12:15:19 records that program (native-binary/claude in the extension folder) as the one doing the access. It lists VS Code as the responsible app because VS Code launched it.

What happened next, from the same log:

  • Your answer: the search paused at the dialog until you answered at 12:15:43. The log records your answer as a denial.
  • Nothing was read: macOS then refused the search's later requests without asking again, and the search finished at 12:15:46. A find -name search only lists file names and never opens files. After the denial it couldn't list anything inside those folders.
  • No repeat: macOS remembers the denial, so the rest of this audit won't bring the dialog back. Nothing in the audit needs other apps' data.

Future agent prompts will say to search only the repo, the session's work folder and the scratchpad. If you ever want macOS to ask VS Code again, tccutil reset SystemPolicyAppData com.microsoft.VSCode should clear the saved answer.

What the bound is on. It is the lower edge of Tesla's Monthly-track incident coverage for the lagged month, 2026-08. The app multiplies it into the low edge of Tesla's effective VMT for August, which is the exposure behind every non-five-day metric.

Where the zero comes from. The coverage for a lagged month is the helmer's share of five-day-track reports, with a band from the pooled share down to the lowest monthly share. Tesla's lowest monthly share is 0/4 (January), so the band's low edge would be 0.

Why zero breaks things. From the ledger (I haven't re-read the code today), the VMT prior is a two-piece log-normal with sigmaLo = ln(best/min)/1.96. A minimum of 0 gives an infinite sigma, and the app also asserts 0 < vmt_min. A zero low edge means "possibly no exposure at all", which that prior cannot express.

  • Tesla's pooled five-day share is about 2 of 15 incidents (≈0.13). Month-by-month shares of 0 reflect tiny counts, not evidence of zero coverage.

  • That touches the density and quantile code, the window-band logic, the zero-VMT handling, and the qual pins that assert 0 < vmt_min.

Yes, the re-pin is fine. Two caveats:

  • Zoox's lag of 0 rests on one on-time month. If its September reports come late, slurp's own rule flips the lag back and stops the run to say so.
  • If Tesla ever does get a real lag, Copilot's bounding question comes back.

What Copilot was doing, step by step:

  1. Since Oct 3, a company whose Monthly reports arrive a release late gets a lag of 1. For such a company, the month before the cutoff is assumed to be missing its Monthly reports. Its completeness is estimated from the company's usual share of crashes that arrive as fast 5-Day reports. For Zoox that was about 60%.
  2. The rule that sets a lag: look at the newest month whose reports could arrive late (now July), and ask whether most of its Monthly reports came on time. A tie counts as late.
  3. Tesla's July had two Monthly reports: one on time, one a release late. That's a tie, so Copilot set Tesla's lag to 1.
  4. That made the model assume Tesla's August was missing its Monthly reports. It tried to estimate how much was in from Tesla's 5-Day share. Tesla files almost everything as Monthly, so that share is 0 in most months. The estimate's floor came out as "possibly none of August is in," which the app can't handle, so slurp stopped and asked how to bound it.
  5. Copilot took that question at face value. It proposed statistical ways to put a floor under the estimate, such as a Beta-distribution bound. That's the "new model."

Why it was the wrong question: Tesla's August reports weren't missing. All 7 are in this release, and Zoox's 3 are too. slurp has a check for exactly that: a lagged month that already holds Monthly reports means the company isn't late, so record the month and set its lag to 0. That check runs after the zero-share check, so Copilot never saw it.

In short, Copilot was estimating how much of Tesla's August was still in the mail when all of it had already arrived. The fix moves that check ahead of the zero-share one, so the stop names the real problem next time.

2. Decision (a)

Yes: keeping every mode and adding Tesla's no-monitor miles as lower bounds is decision (a). But the premise is wrong. The passenger-seat monitors did have a real-time stop:

As far as is known, Waymo and Zoox never had passenger-seat monitors in any miles we count. Waymo's rider-only miles have no staff aboard. Supervised driving at both companies put a safety driver behind the wheel, and our scope already excludes those miles and crashes. Tesla's monitor miles are a setup that Waymo and Zoox data don't contain at all.

The direction of the bias is known even if its size isn't: a crash a monitor prevented never gets filed, so monitor miles can only flatter Tesla. Our data can't size it:

  • Monitor-aboard miles had about 5x fewer crashes per mile in Jan–Jun.
  • But 4 of the 5 no-monitor crashes in that period were other cars hitting a stopped robotaxi, which no stop button prevents.
  • Dallas ran without monitors from launch and has 2.4x Austin's crash rate per mile, which inflates the no-monitor rate.

Checking the numbers behind both possibilities: how the old September estimate was built, how steady Tesla's growth has been, and whether anything in the data argues against the new figures.

The failure was in the old September estimate (480k [300k–720k]). Tesla's own no-monitor miles alone come to 925–972k for September. The July and August estimates held up: both sit inside their old bands, and the old centrals are within 3% of Tesla's no-monitor figures.

Why September was so far off

Tesla's miles were doubling every month. Weekly no-monitor miles grew 12–21% every week from June through September, about 16% a week on average. Monthly totals:

| Month | Tesla no-monitor miles | vs previous month |
|---|---|---|
| Jun | 124k | |
| Jul | 246k | 1.99x |
| Aug | 484k | 1.96x |
| Sep | 972k | 2.01x |

Our own rows already showed the doubling, then assumed it stopped. July and August came from Tesla's Jul 22 and Sep 3 statements and went 240k → 470k. The September row then held August's average daily rate flat (15.2k a day × 30 = 455k, written as 480k). That contradicts the ramp we had just used for August.

The band only allowed up to 1.53x August. It came from the largest and smallest month-over-month ratios in nine months of Tesla's history (1.48x and 0.51x). None of those months were in a sustained growth phase. The largest of nine ratios also isn't a 95% bound.

The Q2 correction overcorrected. In Q2 our estimates for months Tesla hadn't reported yet ran 1.4–2.9x too high, so Tesla's ">10% per week" claim from the Jul 22 call was discounted. It turned out accurate, and Q3's estimates ran about 2x too low. Two quarters missed by about 2x in opposite directions means those bands were far too narrow.

The rule now in the ledger: a month without Tesla data continues the trend of the months that have it, with a band of at least 0.5x–2x around that. Tesla's weekly page data should mostly make guessing unnecessary; October's row will use the measured Oct 1–18 miles.

Is the new mileage correct?

It's Tesla's own count, and no independent mileage source exists. Every consistency check passes:

  • Tesla's two publications agree within 5%.
  • The series reproduces statements Tesla made months earlier: ">380,000" on Jul 22 and "1 million" on Sep 3. It also matches the Q3 deck's "eightfold" and "nearly two million".
  • It's physically plausible. The 195 vehicles riders logged in September would each need 166 miles a day. August implied only 89 a day, so per-vehicle use nearly doubled.

One warning sign: crashes per mile fell sharply in September.

  • Tesla's own crash list has 15 crashes in 957k miles for April–August, but only 6 in 972k miles for September.
  • If the crash rate had held steady, 6 or fewer would happen about 0.7% of the time.
  • The city mix doesn't explain it. At each city's earlier rate, Austin should have had about 10 crashes (it had 3) and Dallas about 6 (it had 3).

Possible explanations, which the data can't separate:

  • Real safety improvement.
  • Safer kinds of added miles, such as Cybercabs or empty repositioning.
  • Tesla counting more kinds of driving as miles than before.
  • Late September reports still to come. Tesla filed one late for July and one for August, but that wouldn't close a gap of about 10 crashes.

If the cause is a broader count, Tesla's September miles-per-incident looks better than it should. September is the latest, partly reported month, so it carries little weight in the app today, but that grows as later months arrive. NHTSA's ~Nov 16 release will publish Tesla's September reports. More than six in scope would mean Tesla's list was incomplete.

Keeping the new rows is recommended: they're the best data available and nothing directly shows a change in what Tesla counts. The crash-rate drop is now a ledger watch item to re-check at the November release. Timing from the clip's frames:

2. Your framing

Agreed: the question is whether a monitor can prevent a would-be crash in real time, and this video shows one doing it. For crashes at speed, which are the ones that injure people, the window is narrower. The person has to notice the problem, decide, and hit a small touchscreen button. Here that took about half a second from reaching to touching, and noticing came before that. Then the car brakes over a couple of seconds. That can catch slowly developing mistakes, not most sudden ones.

The cleanest evidence on injury risk is the no-monitor miles. By our counting rules, those miles have 2 injury incidents in 3.1M miles through Oct 18: the pothole claim, and the Dallas crash where another driver went to hospital. Tesla's page shows 0 because it counts only injuries where the robotaxi made first contact and that Tesla's own investigation backed up, while its human comparison counts every injury crash.

A crash is reportable whenever the system was engaged at any time in the 30 seconds before it. The exception is if those trips ran on FSD (Supervised), the Level 2 system. Then only fatal, hospital-transport, pedestrian/cyclist and airbag crashes get reported, and they go to a file we don't read.

What the research found: no primary source says which system those trips ran, whether their miles are in Tesla's paid-miles chart, when the practice ended, or how many trips there were. Indirect evidence:

  • Elluswamy, Oct 22, 2025: "We continue to operate our fleet in Austin without anyone in the driver's seat, and we have covered more than a quarter million miles with that." Yes, as long as it uses a log scale. In the default window, monthly miles run from 547 (the no-monitor line's January) to 21.4M (Waymo's September), a ratio of about 40,000. On a linear axis every line except Waymo would sit flat on the floor.

On a log axis, equal vertical gaps mean equal ratios, so one chart would show three things no other chart on the page does:

  • Exposure: how much more mileage Waymo has, which is why its intervals are tight and everyone else's are wide.
  • Growth: each line's growth rate, read off its slope.
  • The two Tesla lines: the gap between Tesla's all-modes and no-monitor lines.

  1. Where: a new chart at the top of the Vehicle Miles Traveled section. The per-company charts stay below it unchanged; their linear scales show each line's shape.

Should the per-company charts stay below it (my recommendation), or should the combined chart replace them?

Answering the question first: the confidence intervals don't help here. Then filling your [TODO] with that reasoning, in brackets.

Under Waymo's own definitions, yes: (a) can never exceed (b), and the confidence intervals don't change that. What isn't certain is whether the cause is a bug or an undocumented difference in how the two are built. That's what the email asks.

Why the intervals don't matter here

  • These aren't noisy averages. Each rate is a count of crashed vehicles in the police data divided by the area's human miles.
  • One count contains the other. Every vehicle counted under (a) (its own airbag deployed) is also counted under (b) (some vehicle in its crash had an airbag deploy). The miles are the same, so rate (a) ≤ rate (b) exactly, in every row.
  • What the intervals are for. A 95% interval says how well an observed rate estimates the long-run rate. That matters when comparing independent samples, like Waymo against humans. It doesn't matter for two nested counts from the same records. People wearing red shirts can't outnumber people wearing shirts, whatever the margin of error on either.
  • The Dynamic rows too. They're weighted averages of small-area rates, with the same weights for both outcomes, so the inequality carries through.

What could explain it

  • The two outcomes may come from different fields. For example, (a) from a vehicle-level airbag field and (b) from person-level fields. Then (b) misses some deployments and is understated.
  • (a) may use a different denominator or vehicle filter. That can't be the whole story:
  • In Single Vehicle rows both outcomes count the same vehicles, so their ratio would equal the denominator factor. No other row in that county could exceed it.
  • Los Angeles has 1.16x for Single Vehicle but 2.03x for Pedestrian and 1.77x for Head-on. Travis has 1.25x against 1.76x for Pedestrian.

So your "seeming contradiction" framing is the right register. The six rows with non-overlapping intervals only show the gaps aren't rounding; even San Mateo motorcycles' 1.013x is impossible.

is there effectively a formula we're using in the final forecast section to convert mileage to fleet size? could that be parameterized to give n-day active fleet size, ie, the number of vehicles that have given a ride to a paying customer in the last n days? in particular i care about n=7 but am wondering if that's a staightforward conversion from VMT numbers
03:39 Claude Code claude-opus-5-5 (xhigh) thought for 1m41s · 1m49s wall-clock time

No, the forecast has no such formula. The fleet forecast (FLEET_FORECAST) and the miles forecast (MILES_FORECAST) are written separately. They are linked in one place only: a utilization constant of 180 miles per vehicle per day. It was applied by hand once, in the comment on Tesla's scenario A ([crashla.js:3087-3104](crashla.js#L3087-L3104): 79,669 mi/day ÷ 180 ≈ 440 vehicles, then a slow ramp to a median of 560). It also sets the floor in [tesla-forecast-floor.qual.mjs:20](quals/tesla-forecast-floor.qual.mjs#L20). Waymo and Zoox have no conversion at all.

The parameterization

Let A_n be the number of vehicles that gave at least one paid ride in the last n days, and M_n the fleet's miles over those n days. Then:

A_n = M_n / (n · u_n)

Here u_n is the average miles per active vehicle per day, counting every vehicle that was active at least once for all n days. The equation holds by definition, so all the uncertainty sits in u_n. For any fixed fleet u_n falls as n grows, because occasional and newly added cars count toward A_n while adding few miles. So the formula needs a measured u_7 for each company, and it changes over time.

Why n=7 is not a simple conversion

  1. Utilization varies about 2x, and depends on which fleet is counted. For Tesla in Q2 2026: about 180 mi/day on the ~30 "active" cars; 78 for the same June miles spread over the ~67 cars in the registry; 89 in August and 166 in September using robotaxitracker's count of distinct cars seen in the month. Waymo in September comes out at about 166 (21.4M miles ÷ 30 days ÷ 4,300 cars).
  2. The count depends strongly on n. In August 2026 robotaxitracker counted 64-80 Tesla cars active in the past 7 days against 175 seen in the month, a ratio of about 2.2-2.7. Part of that gap is real: cars rotate in and out, and the fleet doubled that month. Part is an artifact of the tracker: riders log their own trips, so a 30-day window catches more cars than a 7-day one.
  3. "Paid" doesn't match the mileage. Tesla's miles include empty driving between rides, remote-operator recoveries, and possibly employee rides or Cybercab testing (open question 3). A car doing only those adds miles but doesn't count toward A_7.
  4. The miles forecasts are cumulative totals on Jan 1. A fleet size on Jan 1 needs the daily rate on Jan 1, which means assuming a growth path.

A side finding

At 180 mi/day, Tesla's scenario A miles and fleet forecasts disagree:

| Scenario A (miles) | Growth assumed | Miles/day on Jan 1 | Vehicles at 180 mi/day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Floor 9.5M | −7%/week | ~37k | ~206 |
| Central 13M | +5%/week | ~133k | ~740 |
| Ceiling 19M | +15%/week | ~349k | ~1,940 |

The fleet forecast for scenario A has a median of 560 and a 90% range of [290, 1,080]. The two only agree if utilization rises to about 240 mi/day by Jan 1. That's plausible, given how far utilization moved from August to September, but nothing in the code or comments states it.

What would make n=7 workable

  • Tesla: calibrate u_7 from same-week pairs: Tesla's weekly miles from its safety page and robotaxitracker's 7-day active count. That count is a lower bound because it relies on riders logging trips, and the site's robots.txt disallows automated reads of /v1/ and /data/ (open question 8).
